profile.name: Leopold Aschenbrenner
profile.hook: The OpenAI researcher whose AI fund hit $45 billion, then reset
profile.dek: I trace his path from Columbia valedictorian and OpenAI researcher to an AI hedge fund that peaked near $45 billion, then show what the SEC filings reveal about his stake, the July 2026 unwind and what the fund holds now.
profile.answer: Leopold Aschenbrenner net worth is not publicly established. He owns 50% to 75% of Situational Awareness LP, an AI hedge fund adviser that reported $9.28 billion in June 2026 and then lost about 67% in July, but no filing shows his personal fortune.

wealth.basis: Owns 50% to 75% of the adviser, but personal capital, fee income, losses and liabilities are not disclosed
wealth.paragraph: Leopold Aschenbrenner’s net worth is not publicly established as of November 17, 2026. What the filings do show is ownership. The firm’s [June 2026 Form ADV](https://reports.adviserinfo.sec.gov/reports/ADV/333011/PDF/333011.pdf) lists him as chief investment officer and a limited partner owning 50% to 75% of Situational Awareness LP, the adviser, and 75% or more of its general partner. The adviser reported $9.28 billion in regulatory assets, and its [Schedule 13D filings](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2045724/000093583625000543/xslSCHEDULE_13D_X01/primary_doc.xml) say it earns fees based on assets and on realized and unrealized gains. Since then the fund reportedly lost about 67% in July 2026 and shrank to roughly $10 billion, and its [September 30, 2026 Form 13F](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2045724/000093583626000610/xslForm13F_X02/primary_doc.xml) reported just $1.58 billion of listed securities. A large drawdown typically reduces the performance fees an adviser can earn until losses are recovered, but the filings disclose neither the fee terms, his own capital in the fund nor his liabilities. Without those, any dollar figure would be a guess, so I publish none.

sections.heading: Who is Leopold Aschenbrenner?
paragraphs: Aschenbrenner grew up in Germany and graduated as valedictorian of Columbia at 19, according to the introduction to his [June 2024 Dwarkesh Podcast interview](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/leopold-aschenbrenner). His [own biography](https://situational-awareness.ai/leopold-aschenbrenner/) says he then researched long-run economic growth at Oxford’s Global Priorities Institute and later joined OpenAI’s Superalignment team. He lives in San Francisco.

He left OpenAI in April 2024. In the same interview he said OpenAI told employees he was fired for leaking, which he said referred to a brainstorming document he had shared with three outside researchers for feedback. He also said he had been told a memo he wrote warning that OpenAI’s security was inadequate was a reason. That is his account; OpenAI’s internal reasoning is not public.

The two research subjects explain the fund. Growth research asks what can change the scale of the economy; alignment research asks whether powerful AI can be controlled. His investment thesis joins them: if AI keeps improving quickly, the companies that supply chips, memory, data centers and power may gain before the final winners are known. Readers interested in his former employer can see our [OpenAI ownership investigation](/who-owns-chatgpt-openai/).

sections.heading: Situational Awareness: from an essay to a $45 billion peak and a reset
paragraphs: His [June 2024 Situational Awareness essay series](https://situational-awareness.ai/) set out a forecast about AI capabilities, industrial expansion and security, and his biography names Patrick Collison, John Collison, Nat Friedman and Daniel Gross as anchor investors in the firm. The [firm’s website](https://situationalawarenesslp.com/) dates its founding to September 2024 and describes a global equity strategy across technology and energy.

Growth since then is visible in SEC filings. The [first Form 13F](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2045724/000093583625000120/xslForm13F_X02/primary_doc.xml), for December 31, 2024, listed $254.8 million of securities. By June 30, 2026 the table showed $20.24 billion. The more reliable size measure is the [Form ADV](https://reports.adviserinfo.sec.gov/reports/ADV/333011/PDF/333011.pdf) filed June 11, 2026: $9,278,344,000 in regulatory assets across two accounts. Its main fund, Situational Awareness Partners LP, which has an offshore feeder, had 81 investors and a $5 million minimum investment, and the adviser had eight employees.

The same Form ADV shows who owns the business. Aschenbrenner, listed as chief investment officer and a limited partner, owns 50% to 75% of the adviser. Carl Shulman, director of research and co-portfolio manager, owns 25% to 50%, and chief operating officer Nicholas Gross-Whitaker 5% to 10%. Aschenbrenner also owns 75% or more of Situational Awareness LLC, the adviser’s general partner, and the firm’s [Schedule 13D filings](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2045724/000093583625000543/xslSCHEDULE_13D_X01/primary_doc.xml) describe him as its control person.

The firm also takes large stakes in single companies. It reported 5.8% of Core Scientific in August 2025, raised to 9.4% that October before falling to 4.4% by July 2026, 5.6% of Nebius in May 2026 and 21.1% of [SharonAI Holdings](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2045724/000093583626000468/xslSCHEDULE_13D_X02/primary_doc.xml) in August 2026. Those filings say the adviser is paid fees based on assets under management and on realized and unrealized gains.

July 2026 tested the fund. Assets had grown to about $45 billion at the start of the month, a figure that includes borrowed money, [CNBC reported on July 31, 2026](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/31/leopold-aschenbrenner-situational-awareness-fund-fire-sale.html), citing people familiar with the matter. Falling chip and AI stocks triggered margin calls, and the fund sold its leveraged public stock positions, including SK Hynix and CoreWeave, to Citadel at a discount, leaving about $10 billion, much of it private stakes led by Anthropic. An investor letter put the July loss at about 67%, said all leverage had been removed and said the fund was still up about 80% for 2026. Those figures are reported, not filed. The filings do show selling: the [July 2026 Schedule 13D amendment](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2045724/000091957426004796/xslSCHEDULE_13D_X02/primary_doc.xml) cut the Core Scientific stake to 4.4%.

The fund kept investing. Days after the unwind it completed a $400 million private investment, adding to a $100 million stake in the same unnamed company a month earlier, [Investing.com reported on August 6, 2026](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/aschenbrenner-makes-quick-return-after-nearcollapse-of-situational-awareness-4842843), citing Bloomberg; the same report said it kept its stakes in Anthropic, Fluidstack and MatX and quoted Aschenbrenner telling investors the steps let the fund “fight another day.” In September it exercised pre-funded warrants for 2,674,823 SharonAI shares, keeping its 21.1% stake at 8,070,950 shares, according to its [Form 4](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2045724/000093583626000494/xslF345X06/form4.xml). Its [November 16, 2026 Schedule 13G/A](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2045724/000093583626000604/xslSCHEDULE_13G_X02/primary_doc.xml) reported 3.4% of Nebius at September 30, down from 5.6% in May.

sections.heading: An AI thesis expressed through listed infrastructure
paragraphs: The [June 30, 2026 information table](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2045724/000093583626000418/xslForm13F_X02/form13fInfoTable.xml) showed the strategy at its peak: memory suppliers, chip-related businesses, data-center and computing infrastructure, and energy businesses, held almost entirely as shares. The [September 30, 2026 table](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2045724/000093583626000610/form13fInfoTable.xml) keeps the same themes but changes the form: call options on Bloom Energy, Nebius, SanDisk and a memory-chip ETF, plus shares in SharonAI and four smaller miners and power developers. Each table is a quarter-end view of reportable securities; neither is a live list of everything the manager owns.

My reading is that the portfolio expresses an AI buildout thesis through several supply-chain bottlenecks rather than only through model developers. A business can benefit from demand for compute without owning a frontier model. That also creates an important risk: different holdings may depend on the same spending cycle, so having several company names does not necessarily mean having several independent sources of return.

A holdings filing cannot settle whether that risk was hedged. The [SEC’s Form 13F guidance](https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/staff-guidance/frequently-asked-questions-about-form-13f) excludes short positions and explains that an option entry refers to the underlying security. A large put entry is therefore not the premium paid for insurance. Without the terms and the rest of the book, I cannot reconstruct the manager’s net exposure from the table alone.

sections.heading: My finding: the September filing is mostly options, led by one small company
paragraphs: I checked the [September 30, 2026 Form 13F](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2045724/000093583626000610/xslForm13F_X02/primary_doc.xml), filed November 16, against its cover-page total of $1,577,454,028 across 23 entries and nine issuers. Share positions add up to $532,680,878, or 33.8% of the table. The remaining $1,044,773,150, or 66.2%, is call options, reported at the value of the underlying shares: Bloom Energy $389.2 million, Nebius $332.6 million, SanDisk $182.7 million and the Roundhill Memory ETF $140.3 million.

The largest single line is SharonAI Holdings: 8,070,950 shares worth $440,673,870, or 27.9% of the table. That is the same share count the fund reported in September, and its value per share fell from about $84.66 at June 30 to $54.60 at September 30, by my division of the reported values. A company the fund owns about a fifth of now leads its disclosed public book.

The table total fell 92.2% from June’s $20,242,292,228. That number describes the disclosed table, not the fund. It excludes private stakes such as Anthropic, which were reported to make up much of what remained after July, and it counts options at underlying value rather than the premium paid. For comparison, the June table was almost all shares, and SanDisk and Micron alone made up 55.6% of it; neither appears as shares in September.

The practical lesson for a financial investigator is to preserve the unit at every step. Company market capitalization measures a company. A securities table measures disclosed positions under a reporting rule. Fund net asset value measures investor capital after the relevant liabilities. Personal net worth measures one person’s assets less liabilities. A number can be accurate in its original unit and misleading when relabeled.

profile.methodology: I conduct independent document-based research for Visionary Talks. For this profile I read every Form 13F the firm has filed, its June 2026 Form ADV, its Schedule 13D and 13G filings, the founder’s own biography and essays, the firm’s website and his June 2024 podcast interview, plus news reports on the July 2026 unwind, which I label as reported. I calculated concentration and growth figures directly from reported dollar values. Reported holdings, regulatory assets, first-person statements and my interpretation are identified separately. These records do not provide a personal balance sheet, fee rates or audited returns, so I do not turn managed assets into a personal wealth estimate. The research check date is November 17, 2026; financial observations keep their own dates.
notes: No verified personal net-worth observations were established; no historical personal-wealth graph is drawn.
The earlier $400M to $1.6B estimate on this page was an assumption-based model, not a verified dollar range.
Form ADV ownership is reported in bands, not exact percentages.
13F totals include option positions at underlying value and exclude short positions, so they differ from regulatory assets.
13F table values for September 30, 2026 are mostly call options at underlying value; they are not the premium paid and exclude private holdings.

faq.question: Who is Leopold Aschenbrenner?
faq.answer: He is a German-born former OpenAI Superalignment researcher who wrote the June 2024 Situational Awareness essays on AI and then founded Situational Awareness LP, an AI-focused investment firm in San Francisco, in September 2024.

faq.question: How much money does Situational Awareness manage?
faq.answer: Its latest Form ADV, filed June 11, 2026, reported $9,278,344,000 in regulatory assets. After the July 2026 unwind, CNBC reported the fund had about $10 billion left, mostly private stakes. Its September 30, 2026 Form 13F listed $1.58 billion of public securities, mostly call options.

faq.question: Why was Leopold Aschenbrenner fired from OpenAI?
faq.answer: He said on the Dwarkesh Podcast in June 2024 that OpenAI told staff he was fired for leaking, which he said referred to a brainstorming document he shared with three outside researchers. He also said he was told a memo he had written on OpenAI security was a reason. That is his account.

faq.question: Is Leopold Aschenbrenner a billionaire?
faq.answer: No source establishes that. His majority stake in the adviser could be worth a great deal, but a firm’s assets belong to its investors, the fund lost about 67% in July 2026, and the value of his stake depends on undisclosed fees and profits.

faq.question: What stocks does Situational Awareness own?
faq.answer: Its September 30, 2026 Form 13F listed nine issuers: SharonAI shares led at 27.9% of the table, followed by call options on Bloom Energy, Nebius, SanDisk and the Roundhill Memory ETF, plus smaller share stakes in CleanSpark, IREN, Bitdeer and Fermi.
